title: Epidemiology and recurrence of obstructing ureteral calculi in an adult emergency cohort
text:
Epidemiology and recurrence of obstructing ureteral calculi in an adult emergency cohort

BACKGROUND: Obstructing urinary stones are a frequent cause of renal colic and acute kidney injury. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 2,418 adults who presented to emergency departments with CT-confirmed ureteral stones between 2015 and 2021. RESULTS: Mean age was 46.3 years and 63% were men. Stones were located in the distal ureter in 58% of cases, and hydronephrosis was present in 71%. Five-year symptomatic recurrence was 34% (95% CI 31-37). Acute kidney injury occurred in 9% of patients with a solitary kidney. CONCLUSIONS: Obstructing stones are common, frequently recurrent and carry a measurable risk of renal impairment, supporting structured follow-up and metabolic evaluation.

title: Low-dose non-contrast CT versus ultrasound for diagnosing hydronephrosis due to renal calculi
text:
Low-dose non-contrast CT versus ultrasound for diagnosing hydronephrosis due to renal calculi

Renal colic with suspected obstruction requires prompt imaging to guide decompression. We prospectively enrolled 312 patients with flank pain and compared point-of-care ultrasound with low-dose non-contrast computed tomography as the reference standard. Ultrasound detected moderate or severe hydronephrosis with a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 79%, whereas it identified only 54% of stones smaller than 5 mm. The median effective radiation dose of low-dose CT was 1.8 mSv. Combining ultrasound with a plain abdominal radiograph improved stone detection to 72%. Ultrasound is a reasonable first-line test in young patients and pregnant women, while low-dose CT remains preferable when the diagnosis is uncertain or when infection is suspected.

title: Tamsulosin as medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteral stones: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial
text:
Tamsulosin as medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteral stones: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial

BACKGROUND: Alpha-blockers may facilitate spontaneous passage of ureteral stones, but evidence remains inconsistent.
METHODS: In this double-blind trial, 420 adults with a single distal ureteral stone of 5-10 mm were randomized to tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily or placebo for up to 28 days.
RESULTS: Stone passage occurred in 78.6% of the tamsulosin group and 63.3% of the placebo group (risk difference 15.3%, 95% CI 6.5-24.1). Median time to passage was 8 days versus 12 days. Analgesic use was lower with tamsulosin. Dizziness was the only adverse event more frequent with active treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: Tamsulosin increased spontaneous passage of larger distal stones and shortened time to expulsion.

title: Management of obstructing urolithiasis with infection: a review of current guideline recommendations
text:
Management of obstructing urolithiasis with infection: a review of current guideline recommendations

An obstructed, infected collecting system is a urological emergency that requires urgent decompression. This review summarizes current guidelines on the management of obstructing renal and ureteral stones. Recommendations agree that either retrograde ureteral stenting or percutaneous nephrostomy should be performed promptly in patients with fever, sepsis or anuria, with definitive stone treatment delayed until infection has resolved. For uncomplicated stones under 10 mm, observation with analgesia, preferably non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, is appropriate. Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy achieves stone-free rates above 90% for distal stones, while shock wave lithotripsy is less effective for lower pole and hard stones. Hydration, dietary sodium restriction and thiazides or citrate in selected patients reduce recurrence.

title: Household transmission of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in high-burden settings: a prospective cohort
text:
Household transmission of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in high-burden settings: a prospective cohort

Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin and poses a major public health challenge. We followed 1,106 household contacts of 312 index patients with confirmed MDR-TB for 24 months in three high-burden districts. Prevalent disease was found in 3.9% of contacts at baseline, and 14 further cases developed during follow-up, giving an incidence of 0.7 per 100 person-years. Risk was higher among children under five years (adjusted hazard ratio 2.8, 95% CI 1.4-5.6) and among contacts sharing a bedroom with the index patient. Genotyping confirmed an identical strain in 86% of secondary cases. Systematic contact tracing should prioritize young children and close household members.

title: Rapid molecular testing for rifampicin resistance to interrupt transmission of tuberculosis
text:
Rapid molecular testing for rifampicin resistance to interrupt transmission of tuberculosis

BACKGROUND: Delayed detection of drug resistance prolongs infectiousness and facilitates spread of MDR-TB. METHODS: We compared Xpert MTB/RIF testing with conventional culture-based drug susceptibility testing among 1,850 patients with presumptive tuberculosis. RESULTS: Xpert detected rifampicin resistance with a sensitivity of 95% and specificity of 98%. Median time to appropriate treatment fell from 62 days to 4 days. Line probe assays identified additional isoniazid resistance in 37 patients. CONCLUSIONS: Rapid molecular diagnosis shortens the infectious period and should be the initial test for all patients at risk of drug resistance.

title: Six months of levofloxacin as preventive therapy for contacts of patients with MDR-TB: a randomized trial
text:
Six months of levofloxacin as preventive therapy for contacts of patients with MDR-TB: a randomized trial

Evidence for treating latent infection in contacts of MDR-TB patients has been limited. In this double-blind trial, 1,995 household contacts with a positive tuberculin test or a high-risk exposure were randomly assigned to daily levofloxacin or placebo for six months, with follow-up for 54 months. Bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis developed in 6 of 1,000 participants given levofloxacin and 10 of 1,000 given placebo, a non-significant reduction (hazard ratio 0.6, 95% CI 0.3-1.4). Discontinuation owing to musculoskeletal adverse events occurred in 14% of those taking levofloxacin compared with 6% taking placebo. The trial was underpowered, but the direction of effect supports further evaluation of fluoroquinolone-based regimens.

title: Infection control measures to prevent nosocomial spread of drug-resistant tuberculosis: guideline summary
text:
Infection control measures to prevent nosocomial spread of drug-resistant tuberculosis: guideline summary

BACKGROUND: Health care workers and hospitalized patients face increased exposure to drug-resistant tuberculosis.
METHODS: This review summarizes international guidance on administrative, environmental and personal respiratory protection controls.
RESULTS: Recommended measures include prompt triage and isolation of presumptive cases, at least 12 air changes per hour in isolation rooms, upper-room ultraviolet germicidal irradiation, and fit-tested N95 respirators for staff. Surgical masks worn by patients reduce aerosol release. Community-based care lowers hospital exposure.
CONCLUSIONS: Layered controls, rapid diagnosis and early effective treatment are the most effective prevention strategy.

title: Prevalence and malignancy risk of thyroid nodules detected by high-resolution ultrasonography
text:
Prevalence and malignancy risk of thyroid nodules detected by high-resolution ultrasonography

Thyroid nodules are frequently found incidentally, and most are benign. We analyzed ultrasound examinations of 18,740 adults undergoing health screening. Nodules of at least 5 mm were present in 38.2% of women and 24.6% of men, and prevalence increased with age. Among 1,206 nodules that underwent fine-needle aspiration, 6.4% were malignant, predominantly papillary carcinoma. Microcalcifications (odds ratio 5.9, 95% CI 3.8-9.1), irregular margins and a taller-than-wide shape were independently associated with malignancy. The data confirm that sonographic features, rather than size alone, should drive biopsy decisions.

title: Diagnostic performance of fine-needle aspiration cytology and the Bethesda system in thyroid nodules
text:
Diagnostic performance of fine-needle aspiration cytology and the Bethesda system in thyroid nodules

BACKGROUND: Cytology classification guides surgical decision-making for thyroid nodules. METHODS: We reviewed 2,015 ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspirations with histological follow-up in 640 cases. RESULTS: Non-diagnostic samples accounted for 7.8% of aspirates. The risk of malignancy was 3% for Bethesda category II, 22% for category III, 31% for category IV, 76% for category V and 99% for category VI. Molecular testing reduced diagnostic surgery by 41% in indeterminate nodules. CONCLUSIONS: Bethesda categories reliably stratify risk, and molecular testing helps avoid unnecessary lobectomy. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Active surveillance versus immediate surgery for low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma
text:
Active surveillance versus immediate surgery for low-risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma

Overtreatment of small papillary carcinomas is a concern. We compared 1,235 patients with tumors of 10 mm or less who chose active surveillance with 1,090 patients who underwent immediate surgery. Over a median follow-up of 6.1 years, tumor size increased by 3 mm or more in 8% of the surveillance group, and new lymph node metastases appeared in 3.8%. Disease-free survival was 99% in both groups. Permanent hypoparathyroidism occurred in 1.6% of operated patients and vocal cord palsy in 0.9%. Careful ultrasound monitoring every 6-12 months is a safe alternative for selected patients. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Management of thyroid nodules: a review of the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline
text:
Management of thyroid nodules: a review of the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline

BACKGROUND: Clinical management of thyroid nodules ranges from observation to total thyroidectomy.
METHODS: We review recommendations on evaluation, biopsy thresholds, and surgical approach.
RESULTS: Serum thyrotropin should be measured first, and a scan is advised if it is suppressed. Biopsy is recommended for nodules of 1 cm or larger with high-suspicion sonographic patterns, and for 1.5 cm or larger with intermediate patterns. Lobectomy is acceptable for low-risk cancers up to 4 cm.
CONCLUSIONS: Risk-adapted evaluation limits unnecessary biopsy and surgery while preserving oncologic safety. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Prevalence of coarse hepatic echotexture on ultrasound and its relation to fatty liver in adults
text:
Prevalence of coarse hepatic echotexture on ultrasound and its relation to fatty liver in adults

Coarse liver echotexture is a common ultrasound finding of uncertain significance. In a cross-sectional study of 9,860 adults undergoing abdominal ultrasonography, coarse parenchymal echo pattern was reported in 11.4%. Of these, 62% had concurrent steatosis, 18% had viral hepatitis markers, and 9% had excessive alcohol intake. Participants with a coarse pattern had higher alanine aminotransferase (median 48 versus 27 U/L) and a higher FIB-4 index. Independent predictors were body mass index above 28 kg/m2, diabetes and hepatitis B surface antigen positivity. A coarse echotexture should prompt evaluation of metabolic and viral causes.

title: Ultrasound texture analysis versus transient elastography for detecting liver fibrosis
text:
Ultrasound texture analysis versus transient elastography for detecting liver fibrosis

BACKGROUND: Qualitative assessment of a coarse liver pattern is operator dependent. METHODS: We performed B-mode ultrasound and transient elastography in 524 patients with chronic liver disease, with biopsy available in 187. RESULTS: A coarse echotexture predicted significant fibrosis (F2 or greater) with a sensitivity of 68% and specificity of 74%. Liver stiffness above 8.0 kPa achieved an area under the curve of 0.89 (95% CI 0.85-0.93). Combining both approaches improved specificity to 88%. CONCLUSIONS: Elastography should complement conventional imaging when a coarse parenchyma is observed. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Antiviral therapy and regression of fibrosis in chronic liver disease with coarse echotexture
text:
Antiviral therapy and regression of fibrosis in chronic liver disease with coarse echotexture

We conducted an open-label trial in 260 patients with chronic hepatitis B and ultrasonographic coarse liver parenchyma who were assigned to tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg daily or to observation. After 96 weeks, liver stiffness decreased by a median of 2.9 kPa in treated patients compared with 0.4 kPa in controls (P < 0.001). Histological improvement of at least one Ishak stage was observed in 52% of biopsied treated patients. Serum HBV DNA fell below 20 IU/mL in 91%. Treatment was well tolerated, and creatinine remained stable. Antiviral therapy is associated with reversal of early fibrotic changes. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Imaging evaluation of diffuse liver disease: a review of ultrasound findings and follow-up recommendations
text:
Imaging evaluation of diffuse liver disease: a review of ultrasound findings and follow-up recommendations

BACKGROUND: Diffuse changes in hepatic echotexture are nonspecific and require clinical correlation.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the ultrasound patterns of steatosis, chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis.
RESULTS: Increased echogenicity suggests steatosis, whereas coarse texture, nodular surface and caudate hypertrophy suggest advanced fibrosis. Laboratory tests, FIB-4, and elastography are recommended. Patients with cirrhosis should have surveillance ultrasound every six months for hepatocellular carcinoma.
CONCLUSIONS: Integration of imaging with non-invasive fibrosis scores optimizes referral. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Prevalence and causes of elevated aminotransferases in the general adult population
text:
Prevalence and causes of elevated aminotransferases in the general adult population

Elevated serum aminotransferases are commonly found in routine testing. Using data from 12,421 adults in a national health survey, we defined elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) as above 33 U/L in men and 25 U/L in women. The prevalence was 14.3%. Probable causes were non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in 53%, alcohol in 17%, viral hepatitis in 8% and medications in 6%, while 16% remained unexplained. Waist circumference, triglycerides above 1.7 mmol/L and diabetes were strongly associated with high ALT (odds ratio 3.4, 95% CI 2.9-4.0). Metabolic risk factors dominate the etiology. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Diagnostic approach to a patient with raised AST and ALT: pattern recognition and stepwise testing
text:
Diagnostic approach to a patient with raised AST and ALT: pattern recognition and stepwise testing

BACKGROUND: The evaluation of abnormal liver tests is often unfocused. METHODS: We analyzed 1,380 patients referred for persistent aminotransferase elevation and applied a stepwise algorithm. RESULTS: An AST:ALT ratio above 2 suggested alcoholic liver disease with a positive predictive value of 82%. Hepatitis B and C serology, ferritin, autoantibodies and ultrasound established the cause in 79%. Values over 1,000 U/L were mostly due to viral, ischemic or drug-induced injury. CONCLUSIONS: Pattern-based interpretation and targeted tests identify the cause in most patients. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Weight loss and vitamin E for reducing aminotransferases in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a randomized trial
text:
Weight loss and vitamin E for reducing aminotransferases in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a randomized trial

We randomized 240 adults with biopsy-proven steatohepatitis to lifestyle intervention alone, lifestyle plus vitamin E 800 IU daily, or lifestyle plus pioglitazone for 96 weeks. ALT decreased from a mean of 78 U/L to 41 U/L in the vitamin E group and to 38 U/L in the pioglitazone group, compared with 56 U/L with lifestyle alone. Participants who lost at least 7% of body weight showed resolution of steatohepatitis in 58% of cases. Pioglitazone led to a mean weight gain of 2.6 kg. Sustained weight reduction through diet and exercise was the most effective approach to normalize liver enzymes. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Evaluation and management of abnormal liver chemistries: summary of clinical practice guidance
text:
Evaluation and management of abnormal liver chemistries: summary of clinical practice guidance

BACKGROUND: Mild elevations are often transient, yet severe or persistent increases need investigation.
METHODS: This review condenses guideline recommendations from gastroenterology societies.
RESULTS: Repeat testing in 3-6 months is advised for elevations below twice the upper limit. Alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs, including herbal products, should be stopped. Coffee consumption, exercise and the Mediterranean diet are associated with lower ALT. Referral is indicated for jaundice or enzymes exceeding five times normal.
CONCLUSIONS: Addressing metabolic risk and removing toxins normalizes enzymes in most patients.

title: Global prevalence and control rates of hypertension in adults: a pooled analysis
text:
Global prevalence and control rates of hypertension in adults: a pooled analysis

Hypertension remains the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular death. We pooled 1,201 population-based studies covering 104 million participants. The age-standardized prevalence of hypertension, defined as blood pressure of at least 140/90 mm Hg or use of medication, was 32% in women and 34% in men. Only 47% of women and 38% of men were treated, and blood pressure was controlled in 23% and 18% respectively. Prevalence declined in high-income countries but increased in low- and middle-income regions. Improving detection and long-term treatment is essential. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Can primary hypertension be cured? Remission after lifestyle modification and weight loss
text:
Can primary hypertension be cured? Remission after lifestyle modification and weight loss

BACKGROUND: Patients often ask whether hypertension can be permanently cured. METHODS: We followed 380 adults with stage 1 essential hypertension who undertook a structured program of weight loss, sodium restriction below 2 g per day, exercise and the DASH diet. RESULTS: After 12 months, 27% maintained blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg without drugs. Mean systolic pressure fell by 11.4 mm Hg. Remission was more likely with weight loss above 10 kg and younger age; half of those in remission relapsed within three years of stopping lifestyle measures. CONCLUSIONS: Primary hypertension is rarely cured but can be put into remission with sustained lifestyle change.

title: Intensive versus standard blood pressure lowering in high-risk adults: a randomized trial
text:
Intensive versus standard blood pressure lowering in high-risk adults: a randomized trial

We randomized 9,361 non-diabetic adults aged 50 years or older with systolic blood pressure of 130-180 mm Hg and elevated cardiovascular risk to a systolic target of less than 120 mm Hg or less than 140 mm Hg. The trial was stopped early after a median follow-up of 3.26 years. The primary composite outcome occurred in 1.65% per year in the intensive group and 2.19% per year in the standard group (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.64-0.89). All-cause mortality was lower with intensive control. Hypotension, syncope and acute kidney injury were more frequent in the intensive arm. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Secondary causes and curable forms of hypertension: review and diagnostic guidance
text:
Secondary causes and curable forms of hypertension: review and diagnostic guidance

BACKGROUND: A minority of hypertensive patients have an identifiable and potentially curable cause.
METHODS: This review examines renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma and sleep apnea.
RESULTS: Primary aldosteronism affects up to 10% of patients with hypertension, and an aldosterone-to-renin ratio above 30 prompts confirmatory testing. Adrenalectomy cures or improves blood pressure in a majority of unilateral cases. Screening is advised in resistant hypertension or early-onset disease.
CONCLUSIONS: Most patients require lifelong treatment, but identifying secondary causes can lead to cure.

title: Prevalence of symptomatic hemorrhoids and associated risk factors: a population-based survey
text:
Prevalence of symptomatic hemorrhoids and associated risk factors: a population-based survey

Hemorrhoidal disease is among the most common anorectal conditions. We surveyed 4,075 adults aged 20-80 years undergoing colonoscopy screening. Symptomatic hemorrhoids were reported by 38.9%, with a peak between 45 and 65 years. Rectal bleeding was the most frequent complaint (71%), followed by prolapse (34%). Chronic constipation (odds ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.9-3.1), straining, low dietary fiber intake and prolonged toilet sitting were independently associated with the condition. Men and women were equally affected after adjustment for age. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Goligher classification and anoscopic assessment of internal and external hemorrhoids
text:
Goligher classification and anoscopic assessment of internal and external hemorrhoids

BACKGROUND: Accurate grading of hemorrhoids determines treatment. METHODS: We examined 612 patients with anal bleeding by anoscopy and applied the Goligher classification. RESULTS: Internal hemorrhoids were grade I in 29%, grade II in 36%, grade III in 26% and grade IV in 9%. External hemorrhoids and thrombosis were found in 17%. Colonoscopy detected colorectal neoplasia in 4.1% of patients over 50 years, and more often with anemia. CONCLUSIONS: Grading guides therapy, and colonoscopy is advised in older patients to exclude other sources of bleeding. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Rubber band ligation versus hemorrhoidectomy for grade II-III hemorrhoids: a randomized trial
text:
Rubber band ligation versus hemorrhoidectomy for grade II-III hemorrhoids: a randomized trial

We randomized 300 patients with grade II or III internal hemorrhoids to rubber band ligation or conventional excisional hemorrhoidectomy. At 12 months, symptom resolution was achieved in 72% after banding and 94% after surgery (P < 0.001). Postoperative pain scores on day 3 averaged 2.8 versus 6.9 on a 10-point scale, and patients undergoing banding resumed work after a median of 1 day compared with 14 days. Recurrence requiring retreatment was 21% after banding and 4% after surgery. Banding is an appropriate first procedure, while surgery offers more durable results. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Conservative and surgical management of hemorrhoidal disease: a review of guidelines
text:
Conservative and surgical management of hemorrhoidal disease: a review of guidelines

BACKGROUND: Therapeutic options are numerous and rely on symptom severity and grade.
METHODS: This review summarizes society recommendations.
RESULTS: First-line therapy for all grades is increased dietary fiber at 25-30 g per day, fluids and avoidance of straining. Flavonoids reduce bleeding and symptoms. Sclerotherapy and infrared coagulation suit grade I-II disease. Surgery is reserved for grade III-IV or failed office procedures.
CONCLUSIONS: A stepwise approach limits morbidity and costs. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Prevalence of sleep bruxism in children and adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Prevalence of sleep bruxism in children and adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Sleep bruxism is characterized by rhythmic masticatory muscle activity during sleep. We pooled 38 studies including 52,000 participants. The overall prevalence of self-reported sleep bruxism was 13% in adults and 25% in children, declining with age. Associated factors were psychological stress, anxiety, snoring, smoking, caffeine and alcohol intake. Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 87%), reflecting differences in definitions. Polysomnographic confirmation was available in only a minority of studies, and self-report probably overestimates frequency. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Polysomnographic and clinical diagnosis of sleep bruxism with electromyographic recording
text:
Polysomnographic and clinical diagnosis of sleep bruxism with electromyographic recording

BACKGROUND: Reliable diagnosis requires objective measurement. METHODS: We recorded masseter electromyography and audio-video polysomnography in 96 adults with suspected bruxism. RESULTS: Participants with sleep bruxism had a mean of 5.4 rhythmic masticatory episodes per hour, compared with 1.2 in controls. Clinical signs such as tooth wear and masseter hypertrophy had a positive predictive value of 63%. Most episodes occurred in light sleep and were preceded by micro-arousals. CONCLUSIONS: Clinical assessment alone is insufficient to establish severity, and portable electromyography is a useful screening tool. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Botulinum toxin injection versus occlusal splint for sleep bruxism-related pain: a randomized trial
text:
Botulinum toxin injection versus occlusal splint for sleep bruxism-related pain: a randomized trial

We randomized 120 adults with sleep bruxism and masticatory muscle pain to botulinum toxin type A, 60 units into the masseters, or to a custom-made occlusal splint for 12 weeks. Pain intensity on a 10-cm visual analogue scale decreased by 3.9 cm with botulinum toxin and 2.7 cm with splint therapy (difference 1.2 cm, 95% CI 0.4-2.0). Electromyographic activity fell by 38% after injection. Transient chewing weakness occurred in 16% of injected patients. Both therapies were effective, with greater pain relief after botulinum toxin. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Management of bruxism: an international consensus and review of current evidence
text:
Management of bruxism: an international consensus and review of current evidence

BACKGROUND: Management aims to protect teeth and relieve symptoms rather than eliminate grinding.
METHODS: This review is based on an international consensus on assessment of bruxism.
RESULTS: Education, sleep hygiene, stress reduction and avoidance of alcohol and caffeine in the evening are first-line strategies. Occlusal splints protect against tooth wear but do not cure the condition. Cognitive behavioral therapy and biofeedback may reduce frequency. Medications are not recommended routinely.
CONCLUSIONS: Bruxism is viewed as a behavior rather than a disorder unless it causes adverse health consequences. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Prevalence of impacted third molars and associated pathology in young adults
text:
Prevalence of impacted third molars and associated pathology in young adults

Third molar impaction is frequent and may be associated with pericoronitis, caries of the adjacent tooth and cyst formation. We examined panoramic radiographs of 3,260 patients aged 18-30 years. At least one impacted third molar was present in 52.7%, with mesioangular impaction the most common type (41%). Pathology was detected in 28% of impacted teeth, including distal caries of the second molar in 11% and pericoronitis in 9%. Lower molars were affected twice as often as upper molars. Radiographic screening at late adolescence can identify teeth at risk. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Radiographic classification and risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury before third molar extraction
text:
Radiographic classification and risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury before third molar extraction

BACKGROUND: Proximity to the mandibular canal increases surgical risk. METHODS: We evaluated 450 lower third molars with panoramic radiographs and cone-beam computed tomography. RESULTS: Darkening of the root, interruption of the canal wall and diversion of the canal on panoramic imaging were significantly associated with direct contact on CBCT (odds ratio 6.7, 95% CI 3.5-12.8). Temporary sensory disturbance occurred in 3.9% and permanent in 0.6% of extractions. CONCLUSIONS: Cone-beam imaging is advisable when high-risk radiographic signs are present. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Dexamethasone and antibiotic prophylaxis after surgical removal of impacted third molars: a randomized trial
text:
Dexamethasone and antibiotic prophylaxis after surgical removal of impacted third molars: a randomized trial

We randomized 180 patients undergoing lower third molar surgery to submucosal dexamethasone 8 mg, oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for five days, or placebo. On postoperative day two, facial swelling was reduced by 34% in the dexamethasone group relative to placebo, and mouth opening was greater by 7 mm. Alveolar osteitis occurred in 4.4% with antibiotics, 6.7% with dexamethasone and 11.7% with placebo. Pain scores did not differ significantly between groups. Dexamethasone effectively reduced swelling and trismus. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Indications for removal of asymptomatic wisdom teeth: a review of the evidence and guidelines
text:
Indications for removal of asymptomatic wisdom teeth: a review of the evidence and guidelines

BACKGROUND: There is debate about prophylactic removal of disease-free third molars.
METHODS: This review examines randomized trials and guidance documents.
RESULTS: Extraction is indicated for recurrent pericoronitis, caries not amenable to restoration, cysts and resorption of adjacent teeth. Evidence does not support routine removal of asymptomatic teeth, and complication rates rise with age. Coronectomy may lower nerve injury when the roots lie close to the canal.
CONCLUSIONS: Decisions should be individualized, with regular monitoring of retained teeth. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Reference ranges of serum beta-hCG in early normal pregnancy and expected doubling times
text:
Reference ranges of serum beta-hCG in early normal pregnancy and expected doubling times

Serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) is the standard biochemical marker of early pregnancy. We measured quantitative levels in 1,420 women with viable intrauterine pregnancies from 3 to 12 weeks of gestation. Median values were 150 mIU/mL at 4 weeks, 6,500 mIU/mL at 5 weeks and 60,000 mIU/mL at 8 weeks, with wide inter-individual variation. The minimal expected rise over 48 hours was 49% when the initial level was below 1,500 mIU/mL and 40% for levels of 1,500-3,000 mIU/mL. Levels peaked at 8-11 weeks and then declined. Single values must be interpreted in clinical context. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Beta-hCG discriminatory zone and transvaginal ultrasound for diagnosing ectopic pregnancy
text:
Beta-hCG discriminatory zone and transvaginal ultrasound for diagnosing ectopic pregnancy

BACKGROUND: Distinguishing ectopic from early viable pregnancy relies on hormone trends and imaging. METHODS: We prospectively studied 860 women with pain or bleeding in early pregnancy and unknown location. RESULTS: A gestational sac was visible in 99% of viable pregnancies when beta-hCG exceeded 3,500 mIU/mL. An abnormal rise or fall below 35% in 48 hours identified ectopic pregnancy with a sensitivity of 71%. Ectopic pregnancy was ultimately diagnosed in 18% of cases. CONCLUSIONS: A conservative discriminatory threshold of 3,500 mIU/mL reduces the risk of disrupting a viable pregnancy. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy: effect of initial beta-hCG level on treatment success
text:
Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy: effect of initial beta-hCG level on treatment success

We conducted a randomized trial of single-dose versus double-dose methotrexate (50 mg/m2) in 254 women with unruptured ectopic pregnancy and beta-hCG below 5,000 mIU/mL. Treatment success, defined as hCG resolution without surgery, was achieved in 71% with a single dose and 80% with a double-dose protocol (P = 0.12). Success exceeded 90% when baseline hCG was below 1,500 mIU/mL and fell to 58% above 3,000 mIU/mL. A day 4-7 decline of less than 15% predicted failure. Serial hCG monitoring should continue until it is undetectable. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Human chorionic gonadotropin in clinical practice: interpretation of low, high and persistent values
text:
Human chorionic gonadotropin in clinical practice: interpretation of low, high and persistent values

BACKGROUND: Beta-hCG is used in pregnancy confirmation, gestational trophoblastic disease and some tumors.
METHODS: This review addresses interpretation of results.
RESULTS: Abnormally low or slowly rising values suggest ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage, whereas very high levels exceeding 100,000 mIU/mL raise the possibility of molar pregnancy or multiple gestation. Heterophilic antibodies cause false-positive results, and a high-dose hook effect can cause false negatives. Quantitative monitoring after evacuation of a mole is essential.
CONCLUSIONS: Results should be interpreted according to gestational age, trend and imaging.

title: Prevalence and persistence of human papillomavirus infection during pregnancy
text:
Prevalence and persistence of human papillomavirus infection during pregnancy

Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is common in women of reproductive age. We tested cervical samples from 1,850 pregnant women at 10-14 weeks and again in the third trimester. High-risk HPV DNA was detected in 17.6% at the first visit. Among positive women, 58% cleared the virus by 36 weeks, while HPV 16 and 18 persisted more frequently than other genotypes (hazard ratio 0.4 for clearance, 95% CI 0.2-0.8). Age under 25 years and multiple partners were associated with infection. Pregnancy did not appear to accelerate progression to high-grade lesions. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Cervical cytology screening and colposcopy in pregnant women with HPV-positive results
text:
Cervical cytology screening and colposcopy in pregnant women with HPV-positive results

BACKGROUND: Management of abnormal screening in pregnancy aims to exclude invasive cancer while avoiding unnecessary treatment. METHODS: We reviewed 640 pregnant women who underwent colposcopy for abnormal cytology. RESULTS: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse was found in 9.2%, and biopsy was safe in 98% of cases with minimal bleeding. Invasive carcinoma was diagnosed in 0.6%. Regression postpartum occurred in 48% of CIN 2 lesions. CONCLUSIONS: Colposcopy is safe in pregnancy, and treatment of CIN can generally be deferred until after delivery. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Mode of delivery and vertical transmission of HPV: a prospective cohort of mother-infant pairs
text:
Mode of delivery and vertical transmission of HPV: a prospective cohort of mother-infant pairs

Vertical transmission of HPV may occur during vaginal delivery, but the clinical consequences are uncertain. We tested 600 HPV-positive mothers and their newborns for HPV DNA in oral and genital swabs. Neonatal HPV positivity was 11.3% after vaginal birth and 8.6% after cesarean section (relative risk 1.3, 95% CI 0.7-2.4), and most infections cleared by six months. Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis was not observed during follow-up. Cesarean delivery does not eliminate transmission, and HPV infection alone is not an indication for cesarean birth. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: HPV infection in pregnancy: review of vaccination, treatment of genital warts and obstetric recommendations
text:
HPV infection in pregnancy: review of vaccination, treatment of genital warts and obstetric recommendations

BACKGROUND: Counseling pregnant women with HPV requires balancing reassurance and surveillance.
METHODS: This review summarizes current guidance.
RESULTS: Vaccination is not recommended during pregnancy, although inadvertent doses have not been associated with adverse outcomes, and it can be given postpartum. Genital warts may enlarge in pregnancy and can be treated with cryotherapy or trichloroacetic acid, whereas podophyllin, imiquimod and sinecatechins are avoided. Vaginal delivery is preferred unless warts obstruct the birth canal.
CONCLUSIONS: Routine screening schedules should be maintained and follow-up completed after birth.

title: Time to umbilical cord separation and risk factors for delayed detachment in newborns
text:
Time to umbilical cord separation and risk factors for delayed detachment in newborns

Umbilical cord separation typically occurs within the first two weeks of life. We followed 2,140 healthy term newborns from birth until cord detachment. The mean separation time was 8.9 days (SD 3.4), and 6.1% of infants had delayed separation beyond 15 days. Delayed separation was associated with cesarean delivery, application of topical antiseptics, low birth weight and omphalitis. Dry cord care was linked to earlier detachment than chlorhexidine in settings with low infection risk. Persistent moisture or a delay beyond three weeks should prompt evaluation for leukocyte adhesion deficiency. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Diagnosis of umbilical granuloma and omphalitis in the neonatal period
text:
Diagnosis of umbilical granuloma and omphalitis in the neonatal period

BACKGROUND: Moist umbilical stumps can reflect granulation tissue, infection or congenital anomalies. METHODS: We examined 310 neonates referred for persistent wet umbilicus. RESULTS: Umbilical granuloma was present in 74%, omphalitis in 11% with erythema extending beyond the cord base, and patent urachus or omphalomesenteric remnants in 4%. Ultrasound identified urachal remnants in all suspected cases. Staphylococcus aureus predominated in culture-positive omphalitis. CONCLUSIONS: A systematic examination distinguishes simple granulomas from conditions that require surgical or antibiotic therapy. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Topical salt versus silver nitrate cauterization for umbilical granuloma: a randomized trial
text:
Topical salt versus silver nitrate cauterization for umbilical granuloma: a randomized trial

Umbilical granulomas are usually treated by silver nitrate cautery, which can cause chemical burns. We randomized 120 infants with granulomas to application of table salt for 30 minutes twice daily or to a single silver nitrate cauterization. After seven days, complete resolution occurred in 88% of the salt group and 91% of the silver nitrate group (difference 3%, 95% CI -9 to 14). Periumbilical skin irritation was reported in 5% versus 17%, respectively. Salt therapy is a simple, inexpensive and safe alternative that parents can administer at home. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Umbilical cord care in newborns: review of chlorhexidine, dry cord care and guideline recommendations
text:
Umbilical cord care in newborns: review of chlorhexidine, dry cord care and guideline recommendations

BACKGROUND: Cord infection remains a cause of neonatal sepsis in low-resource settings.
METHODS: We reviewed trials of cord antisepsis.
RESULTS: Chlorhexidine 4% applied once daily reduced neonatal mortality by 23% and omphalitis by up to 50% in high-mortality communities. In hospital births in high-income countries, keeping the stump clean and dry, folding the diaper below the cord and avoiding alcohol are recommended. Parents should seek care for fever, pus, foul smell or spreading redness.
CONCLUSIONS: Recommendations depend on baseline infection risk. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Duration and characteristics of lochia after vaginal delivery and cesarean section
text:
Duration and characteristics of lochia after vaginal delivery and cesarean section

Lochia is the vaginal discharge that follows childbirth. We followed 780 postpartum women with daily diaries over eight weeks. Lochia rubra lasted a median of 4 days, lochia serosa until day 22, and lochia alba until day 36, with a total median duration of 34 days (interquartile range 24-45). Discharge lasted longer in breastfeeding women and was shorter after cesarean section by 4 days. Renewed bleeding after initial reduction occurred in 21% of women, usually in the second or third week and coinciding with increased activity. Most episodes resolved without treatment. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Ultrasound evaluation of retained products of conception in women with persistent postpartum bleeding
text:
Ultrasound evaluation of retained products of conception in women with persistent postpartum bleeding

BACKGROUND: Secondary postpartum hemorrhage affects up to 2% of women and requires prompt assessment. METHODS: We examined 215 women presenting 6-42 days after delivery with heavy or recurrent bleeding. RESULTS: Retained placental tissue was identified on ultrasound in 38%, endometritis in 27% and subinvolution in 19%. Endometrial thickness exceeding 10 mm with a vascular echogenic mass had a positive predictive value of 84% for retained tissue. Hemoglobin below 9 g/dL was found in 31%. CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound combined with inflammatory markers directs medical or surgical management. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Misoprostol and antibiotics for secondary postpartum hemorrhage: a randomized controlled trial
text:
Misoprostol and antibiotics for secondary postpartum hemorrhage: a randomized controlled trial

We randomized 190 women with secondary postpartum hemorrhage and ultrasound evidence of minimal retained tissue to misoprostol 600 micrograms sublingually plus amoxicillin-clavulanate, or to antibiotics alone. Complete resolution of bleeding without curettage occurred in 86% of the misoprostol group compared with 64% of the control group (relative risk 1.35, 95% CI 1.14-1.60). Fever and diarrhea were more frequent with misoprostol. The rate of blood transfusion was low in both groups, at 3.2% and 4.2%. Medical management is effective and can avoid surgical evacuation. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Normal and abnormal postpartum bleeding: review of postnatal care guidelines
text:
Normal and abnormal postpartum bleeding: review of postnatal care guidelines

BACKGROUND: Women need clear information on what is expected after childbirth.
METHODS: This review summarizes postnatal care recommendations.
RESULTS: Normal lochia gradually changes from red to pink to yellowish-white and has a fleshy odor without foul smell. Bleeding that soaks a pad within an hour, passage of large clots, fever above 38 degrees Celsius, abdominal pain or foul-smelling discharge require urgent assessment. Rest, hydration and adequate iron intake are advised.
CONCLUSIONS: Early warning signs should be communicated at discharge and at postnatal visits. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Global burden and natural history phases of chronic hepatitis B virus infection
text:
Global burden and natural history phases of chronic hepatitis B virus infection

An estimated 254 million people live with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. This review describes the natural history, which comprises immune-tolerant, immune-active, inactive carrier and HBeAg-negative phases. Annual incidence of cirrhosis is 2-3% among patients with active disease, and the 5-year cumulative risk of hepatocellular carcinoma reaches 10-17% in those with cirrhosis. Progression is influenced by HBV DNA levels, genotype, age at infection, alcohol use and co-infection. Only 10-20% of patients are diagnosed worldwide, and fewer than 5% receive treatment. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Combining HBV DNA, ALT and elastography to determine need for treatment in chronic hepatitis B
text:
Combining HBV DNA, ALT and elastography to determine need for treatment in chronic hepatitis B

BACKGROUND: Defining treatment candidates among patients with moderate viral loads can be difficult. METHODS: We analyzed 1,260 untreated patients with HBeAg-negative infection who had been followed for a median of five years. RESULTS: Patients with HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL and ALT above 40 U/L had a 4.3-fold higher risk of fibrosis progression. Liver stiffness above 9 kPa identified significant fibrosis with an area under the curve of 0.87. About 31% of patients in the so-called gray zone required treatment. CONCLUSIONS: Longitudinal monitoring every 3-6 months and fibrosis assessment help to identify treatment candidates.

title: Tenofovir versus entecavir in treatment-naive chronic hepatitis B: a randomized trial
text:
Tenofovir versus entecavir in treatment-naive chronic hepatitis B: a randomized trial

We randomized 740 treatment-naive adults with chronic hepatitis B to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg or entecavir 0.5 mg once daily for 144 weeks. HBV DNA below 20 IU/mL was reached in 92% of tenofovir recipients and 90% of entecavir recipients. Normalization of ALT occurred in 76% versus 72%. HBsAg loss was uncommon at 1.4% and 1.1%. No resistance was detected over three years. Small decreases in estimated glomerular filtration rate (mean 3.5 mL/min) were noted with tenofovir. Both agents are potent, with similar long-term efficacy. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Chronic hepatitis B management: summary of EASL and AASLD guidance on monitoring and treatment
text:
Chronic hepatitis B management: summary of EASL and AASLD guidance on monitoring and treatment

BACKGROUND: Antiviral therapy suppresses viral replication and decreases complications.
METHODS: This review summarizes international guidelines.
RESULTS: Treatment is recommended for patients with HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL, elevated ALT and moderate fibrosis, and for all patients with cirrhosis and detectable DNA. Nucleos(t)ide analogues with high barrier to resistance are first line. Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with ultrasound every six months is advised for high-risk patients.
CONCLUSIONS: Lifelong follow-up is warranted even after viral suppression. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Reference intervals for white blood cell count and differential in healthy adults
text:
Reference intervals for white blood cell count and differential in healthy adults

Accurate reference intervals are required for interpretation of the complete blood count. We determined intervals from 6,420 healthy adult volunteers using automated hematology analyzers. The reference range for total white blood cell count was 4.0-10.5 x 10^9/L. Median neutrophil proportion was 58%, lymphocytes 31%, monocytes 7%, eosinophils 3% and basophils 0.6%. Lower absolute neutrophil counts were observed in participants of African ancestry, with a lower limit of 1.2 x 10^9/L. Smoking and body mass index were associated with higher counts. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Diagnostic value of leukocyte differential count for bacterial infection versus viral illness
text:
Diagnostic value of leukocyte differential count for bacterial infection versus viral illness

BACKGROUND: Differentiating bacterial from viral illness is a common clinical challenge. METHODS: We evaluated 1,150 febrile patients with microbiologically confirmed diagnoses. RESULTS: White blood cell counts above 15 x 10^9/L and an absolute neutrophil count above 10 x 10^9/L predicted bacterial infection with a specificity of 84%, but the sensitivity was only 52%. A neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio above 10 improved discrimination (area under the curve 0.82). Lymphocytosis was typical of viral infections. CONCLUSIONS: The differential count adds value but should be combined with clinical findings and biomarkers such as C-reactive protein.

title: Evaluation of persistent leukocytosis and leukopenia in adults: a diagnostic approach
text:
Evaluation of persistent leukocytosis and leukopenia in adults: a diagnostic approach

Abnormal white blood cell counts are encountered frequently and have a wide differential diagnosis. We reviewed 980 outpatients with persistent leukocytosis above 11 x 10^9/L or leukopenia below 3.5 x 10^9/L. Reactive causes, including infection, inflammation, corticosteroids and smoking, explained 82% of leukocytosis. Hematologic malignancy was found in 2.7%, particularly with blasts on the smear or counts exceeding 30 x 10^9/L. Leukopenia was most commonly due to drugs, viral infection or benign ethnic neutropenia. A peripheral smear and repeat testing in 4-6 weeks are the first steps. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Management of neutropenia and leukocyte disorders: review of guideline recommendations
text:
Management of neutropenia and leukocyte disorders: review of guideline recommendations

BACKGROUND: Neutropenia increases the risk of serious infection when the absolute neutrophil count falls below 0.5 x 10^9/L.
METHODS: This review addresses evaluation and treatment.
RESULTS: Mild neutropenia between 1.0 and 1.5 x 10^9/L is usually benign. Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency requiring empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within 60 minutes. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor reduces duration of neutropenia after chemotherapy by about 2 days.
CONCLUSIONS: Risk stratification guides outpatient or inpatient management. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Prevalence and patterns of combined oral contraceptive use among women of reproductive age
text:
Prevalence and patterns of combined oral contraceptive use among women of reproductive age

Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are among the most widely used reversible methods. We analyzed survey data from 21,540 women aged 15-49 years in 18 countries. Current use of oral contraceptives was reported by 14.2%, ranging from 2% to 38%. Typical-use failure was 7% in the first year compared with 0.3% for perfect use. Missed pills were reported by 47% of women in the previous cycle, and discontinuation within 12 months was 31%. Younger age and lack of counseling were associated with inconsistent use. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Medical eligibility screening before starting hormonal contraception: blood pressure and thrombosis risk
text:
Medical eligibility screening before starting hormonal contraception: blood pressure and thrombosis risk

BACKGROUND: Safe prescribing of estrogen-containing pills requires screening for contraindications. METHODS: We reviewed 3,050 women initiating combined oral contraceptives in primary care. RESULTS: Elevated blood pressure of at least 140/90 mm Hg was found in 3.1%, migraine with aura in 2.4% and a family history of venous thromboembolism in 4.8%. Smokers aged 35 and above comprised 1.2%. The risk of venous thromboembolism was 3-4 per 10,000 woman-years compared with 1-5 in non-users. CONCLUSIONS: A brief checklist identifies women who should receive progestin-only methods. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Quick start versus conventional start of oral contraceptive pills: a randomized trial
text:
Quick start versus conventional start of oral contraceptive pills: a randomized trial

Starting contraception on the day of the visit may improve continuation compared with waiting for the next menses. We randomized 300 women, after a negative pregnancy test, to quick start on the day of the visit or to start on the first day of the next menstruation. At three months, 77% of the quick start group were still using pills compared with 56% of the conventional group (P < 0.001). Breakthrough bleeding was slightly more common with quick start, 24% versus 17%. No pregnancies occurred in either group. Backup contraception for seven days is advised. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: How to start combined oral contraceptives: summary of clinical guidance on timing, missed pills and drug interactions
text:
How to start combined oral contraceptives: summary of clinical guidance on timing, missed pills and drug interactions

BACKGROUND: Clear instructions improve effectiveness and satisfaction.
METHODS: This review summarizes recommendations from reproductive health organizations.
RESULTS: Pills can be started at any time if pregnancy is reasonably excluded, with a backup method for seven days when started after day five of the cycle. One pill is taken at the same time every day. After one missed pill, take it as soon as possible; after two or more, use condoms for seven days. Rifampicin and some anticonvulsants reduce effectiveness.
CONCLUSIONS: Counseling about side effects such as nausea and spotting improves continuation. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Epidemiology of coronary heart disease and presenting symptoms in women and men
text:
Epidemiology of coronary heart disease and presenting symptoms in women and men

Cardiovascular disease causes about 17.9 million deaths annually. We analyzed presenting features in 22,300 patients with acute coronary syndrome from a national registry. Chest pain was the leading symptom in 82% of men and 71% of women, while dyspnea, nausea, fatigue and back or jaw pain were more common in women. Diabetic patients and older adults more often had atypical presentations. Median delay from symptom onset to hospital arrival was 3.2 hours. Recognition of atypical signs may shorten delays. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of high-sensitivity troponin for myocardial infarction in patients with chest pain
text:
Diagnostic accuracy of high-sensitivity troponin for myocardial infarction in patients with chest pain

BACKGROUND: Rapid exclusion of infarction is important in crowded emergency departments. METHODS: We prospectively enrolled 1,926 patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome and measured high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T at presentation and after one hour. RESULTS: A baseline value below 5 ng/L ruled out myocardial infarction with a negative predictive value of 99.8% (95% CI 99.4-100). The 0/1-hour algorithm classified 62% of patients as rule-out or rule-in. Prevalence of infarction was 15%. CONCLUSIONS: Early troponin algorithms safely expedite triage. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Heart failure signs and symptoms: efficacy of sacubitril-valsartan versus enalapril in reducing hospitalization
text:
Heart failure signs and symptoms: efficacy of sacubitril-valsartan versus enalapril in reducing hospitalization

Dyspnea, orthopnea, edema and fatigue are characteristic symptoms of heart failure. We randomized 8,442 patients with New York Heart Association class II-IV symptoms and an ejection fraction of 40% or less to sacubitril-valsartan or enalapril. After a median follow-up of 27 months, death from cardiovascular causes or hospitalization for heart failure occurred in 21.8% versus 26.5% of patients (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.87). Symptomatic hypotension was more frequent with the combination, whereas renal impairment and hyperkalemia were less frequent. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Recognizing warning signs of heart disease: a review for primary care
text:
Recognizing warning signs of heart disease: a review for primary care

BACKGROUND: Early recognition of cardiac disease decreases morbidity.
METHODS: This review summarizes symptoms that should prompt cardiac evaluation.
RESULTS: Exertional chest pressure, breathlessness, palpitations, syncope, leg swelling and unexplained fatigue are the principal warning signs. An electrocardiogram, natriuretic peptide measurement and echocardiography are the first tests. Chest pain lasting more than 20 minutes with sweating requires emergency transfer.
CONCLUSIONS: Risk factor control reduces the burden of disease. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Prevalence of migraine across the female life course and its relation to hormonal fluctuations
text:
Prevalence of migraine across the female life course and its relation to hormonal fluctuations

Migraine is about three times more common in women than in men. We analyzed a population survey of 18,500 women aged 18-65 years. Twelve-month prevalence was 17.1%, peaking at 24.5% in women aged 30-39 years. Menstrually related migraine affected 38% of women with migraine, and attacks were longer and more disabling than non-menstrual episodes. Symptoms often improved during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy in 60-70% of women and worsened at perimenopause. Migraine with aura was associated with a doubled risk of ischemic stroke (hazard ratio 2.1, 95% CI 1.4-3.2). These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Diagnostic criteria and differentiating features of migraine with and without aura
text:
Diagnostic criteria and differentiating features of migraine with and without aura

BACKGROUND: Misdiagnosis delays effective treatment. METHODS: We applied ICHD-3 criteria to 940 women presenting with recurrent headache. RESULTS: Migraine was diagnosed in 61%, of whom 27% reported aura. Unilateral location, pulsating quality, nausea and photophobia had positive predictive values of 70-85%. Tension-type headache accounted for 24% and medication-overuse headache for 8%. Neuroimaging was normal in all 112 patients who underwent MRI without red flags. CONCLUSIONS: A structured history is sufficient for diagnosis in most cases, and imaging is reserved for atypical features. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Erenumab for prevention of episodic migraine in women: a randomized, double-blind trial
text:
Erenumab for prevention of episodic migraine in women: a randomized, double-blind trial

We randomized 955 adults, of whom 85% were women, with 4-14 migraine days per month to erenumab 70 mg, 140 mg or placebo, given monthly for 24 weeks. The mean reduction in monthly migraine days was 3.2 days with 70 mg, 3.7 days with 140 mg and 1.8 days with placebo (P < 0.001 for both doses). A reduction of at least 50% was achieved in 43%, 50% and 27% of patients, respectively. Constipation and injection-site reactions were the most frequent adverse events. Efficacy was similar in premenopausal and postmenopausal women. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Management of migraine in women: guideline review including contraception, pregnancy and acute treatment
text:
Management of migraine in women: guideline review including contraception, pregnancy and acute treatment

BACKGROUND: Management of migraine in women has to consider reproductive status.
METHODS: We summarize recommendations from neurological societies.
RESULTS: Triptans and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are first-line for acute attacks, with acetaminophen preferred in pregnancy. Estrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated in migraine with aura because of stroke risk. Preventive options include propranolol, topiramate and amitriptyline, though topiramate and valproate should be avoided in women planning pregnancy.
CONCLUSIONS: Individualized therapy and a headache diary improve outcomes. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Prevalence of varicocele and testicular size discrepancy in adolescents and young men
text:
Prevalence of varicocele and testicular size discrepancy in adolescents and young men

Varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility. We performed scrotal examination and ultrasonography in 3,420 males aged 12-25 years. Clinical varicocele was present in 14.8%, predominantly on the left side (92%). Testicular volume differed by at least 20% between sides in 9.6% of participants, and in 47% of those with grade III varicocele. Semen analysis in men over 18 years showed lower mean sperm concentration with varicocele (31 versus 52 million/mL). Asymmetry should prompt systematic evaluation. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography for diagnosis and grading of varicocele
text:
Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography for diagnosis and grading of varicocele

BACKGROUND: Physical examination may under- or overestimate varicocele. METHODS: We compared clinical grading with color Doppler ultrasonography in 285 men. RESULTS: Doppler found venous diameters above 3 mm in 91% of men with clinical varicoceles and detected subclinical varicocele in 12% of men with normal examination. Reflux on Valsalva maneuver correlated with testicular hypotrophy (r = 0.58). Testicular volume was measured with the ellipsoid formula, and a difference above 2 mL was abnormal in adolescents. CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound adds value to physical examination when the findings are unclear. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy versus observation in adolescents with testicular volume loss: a randomized trial
text:
Microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy versus observation in adolescents with testicular volume loss: a randomized trial

We randomized 160 adolescents with grade II-III left varicocele and at least 15% testicular volume discrepancy to microsurgical varicocelectomy or observation for 24 months. Catch-up growth of the left testis occurred in 78% of operated adolescents and 26% of controls (P < 0.001). Mean left testicular volume increased by 4.3 mL versus 1.1 mL. Hydrocele occurred in 2.5% after surgery and no testicular atrophy was observed. Surgery restores symmetric growth in adolescents with significant volume loss. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Evaluation of testicular asymmetry and varicocele: review of urological recommendations
text:
Evaluation of testicular asymmetry and varicocele: review of urological recommendations

BACKGROUND: Asymmetry in testicle size is frequently normal, because the left testis often hangs lower and may be slightly larger.
METHODS: This review summarizes when evaluation is necessary.
RESULTS: Further assessment is indicated for a painless mass, hard testis, sudden swelling, volume loss, or infertility. Ultrasound can exclude tumor, hydrocele or torsion. Treatment of varicocele is recommended for infertility with abnormal semen parameters, persistent pain or progressive testicular hypotrophy in adolescents.
CONCLUSIONS: Observation is acceptable for asymptomatic men with normal volumes. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Resurgence of measles and vaccine coverage gaps: epidemiological surveillance, 2015-2023
text:
Resurgence of measles and vaccine coverage gaps: epidemiological surveillance, 2015-2023

Measles outbreaks have resurged where immunization coverage falls below the 95% threshold required for herd protection. We analyzed national surveillance data from 41 countries. Incidence rose from 12 to 47 cases per million, with 61% of cases occurring in unvaccinated individuals and 19% in those who had received only one dose. Infants under 12 months accounted for 16% of cases. Complications included pneumonia in 8% and encephalitis in 0.1%. Closing gaps in two-dose coverage is the main preventive priority. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Measles antibody seroprevalence after one and two doses of MMR vaccine
text:
Measles antibody seroprevalence after one and two doses of MMR vaccine

BACKGROUND: Waning immunity may contribute to breakthrough infection. METHODS: We measured measles IgG by enzyme immunoassay in 1,640 children and young adults. RESULTS: Seropositivity (IgG above 16.5 mIU/mL) was 92% after one dose and 98.5% after two doses. Geometric mean titers declined from 3,200 to 1,100 mIU/mL over ten years. Children vaccinated before 12 months had lower seroconversion rates (84%). CONCLUSIONS: Two doses provide durable protection, and vaccination before 12 months should not count as a valid dose. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Immunogenicity and safety of a monovalent measles vaccine booster after MMR in children: a randomized trial
text:
Immunogenicity and safety of a monovalent measles vaccine booster after MMR in children: a randomized trial

In outbreak settings, an additional early dose of measles-containing vaccine is sometimes administered. We randomized 420 children aged 12-24 months who had received one MMR dose to a monovalent measles vaccine or to a second MMR dose, with 28-day follow-up. Seroconversion for measles was 99% in both groups, and geometric mean titers were comparable (4,150 versus 4,380 mIU/mL). Fever occurred in 9% and 10%, and rash in 3% and 4%. No serious vaccine-related adverse events were observed. The single-antigen vaccine is immunogenic and safe when used after MMR. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccination schedules and catch-up recommendations: a review
text:
Measles, mumps and rubella vaccination schedules and catch-up recommendations: a review

BACKGROUND: Optimal timing and dosing of MMR are determined by outbreak risk.
METHODS: This review compares schedules from international health authorities.
RESULTS: The first dose is given at 12-15 months and the second at 4-6 years, with a minimum interval of 28 days. During outbreaks, infants aged 6-11 months can receive an early dose that is not counted. Contraindications include pregnancy, severe immunosuppression and anaphylaxis to vaccine components. Adults born after 1957 without evidence of immunity should receive two doses.
CONCLUSIONS: Vaccine safety is well established, and there is no association with autism.

title: Incidence of end-stage renal disease and access to kidney transplantation: a registry analysis
text:
Incidence of end-stage renal disease and access to kidney transplantation: a registry analysis

End-stage renal disease (ESRD) imposes a large burden worldwide. We analyzed registry data from 126,000 patients starting renal replacement therapy between 2010 and 2020. Incidence was 164 per million population, and diabetes was the leading cause (38%). Only 21% of patients were placed on the waiting list within one year, with lower access among older, female and lower-income patients. Median waiting time for a deceased donor kidney was 3.9 years. Five-year survival was 86% with transplantation versus 41% with maintenance hemodialysis. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Pre-transplant evaluation and immunological risk assessment in candidates with ESRD
text:
Pre-transplant evaluation and immunological risk assessment in candidates with ESRD

BACKGROUND: Comprehensive evaluation optimizes allocation and outcomes. METHODS: We reviewed 1,030 candidates evaluated at a transplant center. RESULTS: Cardiovascular screening revealed significant coronary stenosis in 17%, malignancy in 2.1% and active infection in 4.6%. Panel-reactive antibody above 80% was found in 12%. HLA mismatch at three or more loci increased the risk of rejection (odds ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.3-2.8). CONCLUSIONS: Systematic assessment identifies modifiable risks and sensitized patients who need desensitization or paired exchange. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Belatacept versus tacrolimus-based immunosuppression after kidney transplantation: a randomized trial
text:
Belatacept versus tacrolimus-based immunosuppression after kidney transplantation: a randomized trial

We randomized 666 recipients of deceased or living donor kidneys to belatacept or tacrolimus in combination with mycophenolate and corticosteroids. At 36 months, graft survival was 92% with belatacept and 89% with tacrolimus, and estimated glomerular filtration rate was higher with belatacept (65 versus 50 mL/min per 1.73 m2). Acute rejection occurred in 22% and 14%, respectively. Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder was observed in 1.8% of belatacept recipients, mostly EBV-seronegative patients. Belatacept improves renal function but requires careful patient selection. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Kidney transplantation for patients with chronic kidney failure: review of guidelines on timing, donor selection and long-term care
text:
Kidney transplantation for patients with chronic kidney failure: review of guidelines on timing, donor selection and long-term care

BACKGROUND: Transplantation is the treatment of choice for suitable patients with ESRD.
METHODS: This review summarizes KDIGO recommendations.
RESULTS: Preemptive transplantation, before dialysis, is advised when the eGFR is below 15 mL/min per 1.73 m2. Living donation offers better long-term graft survival, with a median graft half-life of 15-20 years. After transplantation, lifelong immunosuppression, monitoring of trough levels, infection prophylaxis and cardiovascular risk control are needed.
CONCLUSIONS: Referral should occur early, ideally at an eGFR of 20-30 mL/min. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Prevalence of Helicobacter pylori infection and endoscopic findings of erosive gastritis and duodenal ulcer
text:
Prevalence of Helicobacter pylori infection and endoscopic findings of erosive gastritis and duodenal ulcer

Helicobacter pylori infection is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease. We analyzed 8,960 upper endoscopies performed for dyspepsia. Erosive gastritis was found in 17.5%, duodenal ulcer in 6.3% and reflux esophagitis in 11.8%. H. pylori was detected by histology in 54% overall and in 88% of patients with duodenal ulcer. Use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs increased risk of gastric erosions (odds ratio 3.7, 95% CI 2.9-4.7). Eradication of infection is therefore central to ulcer management. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of urea breath test and stool antigen for Helicobacter pylori infection
text:
Diagnostic accuracy of urea breath test and stool antigen for Helicobacter pylori infection

BACKGROUND: Non-invasive tests are preferred for diagnosis and confirmation of eradication. METHODS: We evaluated 740 patients with dyspepsia using histology and culture as the reference standard. RESULTS: The urea breath test had a sensitivity of 95% and specificity of 96%, and the stool antigen test had 92% and 94%. Proton pump inhibitors reduced sensitivity by 10-15% when taken within two weeks before testing. Serology was less specific in patients with previous treatment. CONCLUSIONS: Proton pump inhibitors should be withheld for two weeks before testing. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Bismuth quadruple therapy versus clarithromycin triple therapy for Helicobacter pylori eradication: a randomized trial
text:
Bismuth quadruple therapy versus clarithromycin triple therapy for Helicobacter pylori eradication: a randomized trial

We randomized 680 patients with H. pylori infection and endoscopically confirmed duodenal ulcer or gastritis to 14 days of bismuth quadruple therapy or standard triple therapy with clarithromycin, amoxicillin and a proton pump inhibitor. In intention-to-treat analysis, eradication rates were 89% and 76% (difference 13%, 95% CI 8-18). Clarithromycin resistance, present in 22% of isolates, reduced the success of triple therapy to 48%. Adverse events such as metallic taste and dark stools were more frequent with quadruple therapy, but adherence was similar. Ulcer healing at eight weeks reached 94%. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Management of peptic ulcer disease and erosive gastritis: summary of the American College of Gastroenterology guideline
text:
Management of peptic ulcer disease and erosive gastritis: summary of the American College of Gastroenterology guideline

BACKGROUND: Gastric acid suppression and eradication of H. pylori heal most ulcers.
METHODS: This review summarizes guidelines for management of ulcers and gastritis.
RESULTS: Proton pump inhibitors are given for 4-8 weeks, with the cause addressed by stopping NSAIDs and treating H. pylori. Upper endoscopy is recommended for alarm features such as bleeding, weight loss, anemia or age over 60 years. Smoking cessation and alcohol reduction improve healing.
CONCLUSIONS: Eradication lowers ulcer recurrence from 60% to under 10% at one year. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Prevalence of dental caries and gingival bleeding in adults: a national oral health survey
text:
Prevalence of dental caries and gingival bleeding in adults: a national oral health survey

Dental caries and gingivitis remain among the most common chronic conditions. We examined 5,820 adults aged 20-64 years. Untreated caries was found in 31.2%, with mean decayed, missing and filled teeth (DMFT) of 8.4. Bleeding on probing was recorded in 58% of participants, and periodontal pockets of at least 4 mm in 34%. Toothbrushing less than twice daily, smoking, diabetes and sugary snacks between meals were independently associated with disease. Only 41% reported having a dental visit in the previous year. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Clinical and radiographic detection of caries: comparison of visual inspection with bitewing radiographs
text:
Clinical and radiographic detection of caries: comparison of visual inspection with bitewing radiographs

BACKGROUND: Early detection of carious lesions permits non-operative management. METHODS: We compared the ICDAS visual examination with bitewing radiography in 380 patients. RESULTS: Visual inspection detected cavitated lesions with a sensitivity of 74% and specificity of 94%, while bitewings detected proximal lesions missed in 29% of cases. Dark discoloration and a hole in the enamel corresponded to dentin involvement in 86% of cases. CONCLUSIONS: Radiographs should complement clinical examination for interproximal surfaces. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Fluoride varnish and chlorhexidine mouthwash for caries arrest and gingival bleeding: a randomized trial
text:
Fluoride varnish and chlorhexidine mouthwash for caries arrest and gingival bleeding: a randomized trial

We randomized 560 adults with active caries and gingivitis to professional application of 5% sodium fluoride varnish every 3 months plus home use of 0.12% chlorhexidine rinse, or to standard care with oral hygiene instruction. After 12 months, the mean number of new carious lesions was 0.7 versus 1.9 (P < 0.001), and the proportion of sites with bleeding on probing fell from 52% to 19% versus 49% to 33%. Extrinsic tooth staining was reported by 14% using chlorhexidine. Combined preventive treatment effectively reduces caries incidence and gingival inflammation. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Prevention and treatment of caries and gingivitis: review of evidence-based oral hygiene recommendations
text:
Prevention and treatment of caries and gingivitis: review of evidence-based oral hygiene recommendations

BACKGROUND: Gingival bleeding is usually caused by plaque-induced inflammation.
