METHODS: This review summarizes the evidence.
RESULTS: Brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste containing 1,000-1,500 ppm, daily interdental cleaning and limiting free sugars to under 10% of energy are the key behaviors. Bleeding that persists after two weeks of improved hygiene, along with mobility or a systemic disease such as diabetes or leukemia, requires dental or medical review. Restorations are required for cavitated lesions.
CONCLUSIONS: Regular dental checks every 6-12 months enable early intervention. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Prevalence of intermittent explosive disorder and anger problems in the general population
text:
Prevalence of intermittent explosive disorder and anger problems in the general population

Anger attacks and impulsive aggression are associated with considerable impairment. We interviewed 9,282 adults in a nationally representative psychiatric epidemiology survey. Lifetime intermittent explosive disorder was identified in 5.4% and 12-month prevalence in 2.6%. Onset occurred at a median age of 14 years. The disorder was associated with depression, anxiety, substance use and chronic pain, with odds ratios of 2.5-4.0. Only 29% of affected persons had sought treatment in the past year, and few received an evidence-based intervention. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Assessment of anger and irritability using the State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory in adults
text:
Assessment of anger and irritability using the State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory in adults

BACKGROUND: Structured instruments help clinicians to quantify anger and plan treatment. METHODS: We administered the State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory-2 to 420 adults with mood or stress-related complaints and 380 community controls. RESULTS: Trait anger scores averaged 24.6 in patients versus 17.2 in controls (P < 0.001), and scores above 28 were found in 31% of the clinical group. Sleep deprivation and alcohol use predicted higher scores. The inventory had an internal consistency of 0.89. CONCLUSIONS: Routine screening can identify those who need psychological intervention. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Cognitive behavioral therapy for anger: a randomized controlled trial of a 12-session program
text:
Cognitive behavioral therapy for anger: a randomized controlled trial of a 12-session program

We randomized 150 adults with problematic anger to a 12-week group cognitive behavioral therapy program including relaxation training, cognitive restructuring and communication skills, or to a waitlist. After treatment, the mean reduction in trait anger score was 8.1 points in the therapy group and 1.9 points in the waitlist group (difference 6.2, 95% CI 4.3-8.1). Aggressive incidents reported per month fell from 5.2 to 1.6. Gains persisted at six months in 78% of participants. Therapy was effective and well accepted, with a dropout of 12%. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Managing difficulty with anger and emotional regulation: review of psychological and pharmacological approaches
text:
Managing difficulty with anger and emotional regulation: review of psychological and pharmacological approaches

BACKGROUND: Difficulty controlling anger may reflect stress, depression, trauma or neurodevelopmental disorders.
METHODS: This review summarizes strategies.
RESULTS: Identifying triggers, taking a time-out, breathing exercises, regular physical activity and adequate sleep are helpful self-management techniques. Mindfulness-based programs reduce reactivity. SSRIs such as fluoxetine can reduce impulsive aggression in selected patients. Referral is advised if anger leads to violence or harms relationships.
CONCLUSIONS: Treatment of underlying conditions is essential. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Squamous cell carcinoma antigen levels in healthy individuals and benign skin and lung conditions
text:
Squamous cell carcinoma antigen levels in healthy individuals and benign skin and lung conditions

Squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCC-Ag) is a serum marker used for cervical, head and neck, lung and esophageal squamous carcinomas. We measured SCC-Ag by chemiluminescent immunoassay in 2,100 healthy adults and 640 patients with benign diseases. The 95th percentile in healthy persons was 1.5 ng/mL. Values above 1.5 ng/mL occurred in 24% of patients with psoriasis or eczema, 17% with renal failure and 9% with benign lung disease. Contamination of samples with saliva or sweat caused false elevations. Interpretation requires knowledge of benign causes. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex.

title: Serum SCC antigen for monitoring recurrence in cervical squamous cell carcinoma
text:
Serum SCC antigen for monitoring recurrence in cervical squamous cell carcinoma

BACKGROUND: Posttreatment surveillance of cervical cancer depends on early detection of recurrence. METHODS: We followed 412 women treated with chemoradiation for stage IB-IVA squamous cervical cancer, with SCC-Ag measured every three months. RESULTS: Elevated SCC-Ag preceded clinical or radiological recurrence by a median of 4.1 months. A threshold of 2.0 ng/mL yielded sensitivity of 76% and specificity of 91% for recurrence. Pretreatment levels above 10 ng/mL predicted lymph node involvement (odds ratio 4.6, 95% CI 2.7-7.8). CONCLUSIONS: SCC-Ag is a useful adjunct to imaging in follow-up. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Prognostic value of pretreatment SCC antigen in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma treated with chemoradiotherapy
text:
Prognostic value of pretreatment SCC antigen in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma treated with chemoradiotherapy

We prospectively measured SCC antigen before treatment in 288 patients with locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Median value was 2.3 ng/mL, and 41% had elevated levels. Patients with levels above 3.0 ng/mL had inferior 3-year progression-free survival (48% versus 71%; hazard ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.3-2.8) and overall survival (57% versus 79%). A decline of more than 50% after treatment predicted complete response in 83% of cases. SCC-Ag provides independent prognostic information alongside stage and HPV status. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Tumor markers in squamous cell cancers: review of SCC antigen utility and guideline recommendations
text:
Tumor markers in squamous cell cancers: review of SCC antigen utility and guideline recommendations

BACKGROUND: Tumor markers support, but cannot replace, histopathology and imaging.
METHODS: This review assesses the role of SCC antigen.
RESULTS: SCC-Ag is not recommended as a screening test because of low sensitivity of 30-60% for early disease and false-positive results in benign skin, kidney and respiratory conditions. Guidelines endorse use for baseline staging and surveillance in cervical cancer. A rising trend on two consecutive measurements should prompt imaging.
CONCLUSIONS: Results must be considered together with clinical findings. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.

title: Prevalence and duration of post-infectious fatigue after acute febrile illness in adults
text:
Prevalence and duration of post-infectious fatigue after acute febrile illness in adults

Fatigue after acute infection is common but poorly characterized. We followed 1,320 adults who had a febrile illness caused by influenza, dengue or other infection for six months. Clinically significant fatigue, defined as a Fatigue Severity Scale score above 4, was present in 42% at two weeks, 19% at three months and 8% at six months. Female sex, severe acute illness, prolonged fever of more than five days and pre-existing depression were risk factors. Most patients recovered spontaneously, with a median time to resolution of nine weeks. These data may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future prospective research.

title: Laboratory evaluation of persistent weakness after fever: when to look for anemia, thyroid disease and ongoing infection
text:
Laboratory evaluation of persistent weakness after fever: when to look for anemia, thyroid disease and ongoing infection

BACKGROUND: Persistent weakness following fever may have a treatable cause. METHODS: We evaluated 360 patients presenting with prolonged fatigue four weeks after a febrile illness. RESULTS: Routine tests identified anemia in 14%, vitamin D deficiency in 28%, thyroiditis in 3.6% and subclinical hypothyroidism in 6%. C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L suggested persistent inflammation or infection in 7%. Electrolyte disturbances were rare at 2%. No cause was found in 52%. CONCLUSIONS: A limited laboratory panel is sufficient initially. Cost-effectiveness and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed and merit separate evaluation.

title: Graded exercise and nutritional rehabilitation for fatigue after acute viral illness: a randomized trial
text:
Graded exercise and nutritional rehabilitation for fatigue after acute viral illness: a randomized trial

We randomized 180 adults with fatigue lasting more than four weeks after an acute febrile viral infection to a 12-week program of graded aerobic exercise with dietary counseling or to usual advice. Mean Fatigue Severity Scale score fell from 5.6 to 3.1 in the intervention group and from 5.5 to 4.4 in controls (difference 1.3, 95% CI 0.8-1.8). The six-minute walking distance increased by 62 m versus 18 m. Adverse events were minor. Gradual return to activity with adequate protein, hydration and sleep accelerates recovery. The authors recommend that clinicians individualize decisions according to patient preference and comorbidity.

title: Approach to post-viral fatigue and convalescence: review of clinical recommendations
text:
Approach to post-viral fatigue and convalescence: review of clinical recommendations

BACKGROUND: Weakness after fever reflects catabolism, deconditioning and immune activation.
METHODS: This review summarizes management.
RESULTS: Reassurance, adequate sleep of 7-9 hours, balanced diet with 1.0-1.2 g/kg of protein, hydration and progressive activity are recommended. Pacing is advised to avoid relapse. Fatigue lasting beyond six months, associated with unrefreshing sleep and post-exertional malaise, should prompt assessment for myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome.
CONCLUSIONS: Supplements are of unproven benefit in the absence of deficiency. Limitations include the observational design and the possibility of residual confounding.

title: Incidence of anti-tuberculosis drug-induced hepatotoxicity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Incidence of anti-tuberculosis drug-induced hepatotoxicity: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Hepatotoxicity is a serious adverse effect of first-line antituberculosis therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide. We pooled 42 cohort studies including 18,600 patients. The pooled incidence of drug-induced liver injury was 11.2% (95% CI 8.9-13.7), with severe hepatitis requiring discontinuation in 2.8%. Risk factors included age over 60 years, female sex, hypoalbuminemia, chronic hepatitis B or C, alcohol use and slow NAT2 acetylator genotype. Most events occurred within the first eight weeks of treatment. Findings were consistent across prespecified subgroups defined by age and sex. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Definition and monitoring of liver injury during tuberculosis treatment: aminotransferase thresholds
text:
Definition and monitoring of liver injury during tuberculosis treatment: aminotransferase thresholds

BACKGROUND: Early recognition limits harm from antituberculosis drug hepatitis. METHODS: We analyzed monitoring data from 2,480 patients receiving standard four-drug therapy. RESULTS: Aminotransferase elevations to above three times the upper limit with symptoms, or above five times without symptoms, were observed in 6.4%. Bilirubin above 2 mg/dL with elevated ALT indicated a worse outlook, with 9% mortality. Baseline monitoring at weeks 2, 4 and 8 detected 91% of events. CONCLUSIONS: Regular liver tests guide timely interruption of hepatotoxic drugs. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations.

title: Reintroduction regimens after antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis: a randomized comparison of sequential and simultaneous rechallenge
text:
Reintroduction regimens after antituberculosis drug-induced hepatitis: a randomized comparison of sequential and simultaneous rechallenge

We randomized 210 patients who recovered from drug-induced hepatitis, defined as ALT below twice the upper limit of normal, to sequential reintroduction of rifampicin, isoniazid and then pyrazinamide at three-day intervals or to simultaneous reintroduction of all drugs. Recurrent hepatitis developed in 8.6% of the sequential group and 17.1% of the simultaneous group (relative risk 0.5, 95% CI 0.2-0.98). The pyrazinamide was implicated most frequently. Treatment completion rates were 94% and 90%. Stepwise rechallenge is safer and enables completion of therapy in most patients. Results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity between participating centers.

title: Management of antituberculosis drug-induced liver injury: review of guideline recommendations
text:
Management of antituberculosis drug-induced liver injury: review of guideline recommendations

BACKGROUND: Hepatotoxicity requires balancing safety and effective treatment.
METHODS: This review summarizes ATS, WHO and national guidelines.
RESULTS: Hepatotoxic drugs should be stopped when ALT exceeds five times the upper limit or three times with symptoms. Non-hepatotoxic regimens containing ethambutol, a fluoroquinolone and an aminoglycoside can be used temporarily. Alcohol should be avoided, and patients with chronic liver disease need more frequent testing. Silymarin and N-acetylcysteine have inconsistent evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Drugs are reintroduced sequentially once liver tests normalize. Sensitivity analyses excluding incomplete records did not materially change the estimates.
